title: Be Strong and Courageous: Joshua Takes Command
summary: After Moses' death the LORD commands Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan into the land he is giving them, promising to be with him as he was with Moses. God charges him to be strong and courageous and to keep the Book of the Law in his mouth, meditating on it day and night. Joshua orders the people to prepare to cross in three days and reminds the eastern tribes of their promise to fight alongside their brothers, and they pledge to obey him.
story: Deuteronomy ended with Moses dead on Mount Nebo and Joshua filled with the spirit of wisdom. The book of Joshua opens on the same spot. Israel is still camped on the plains of Moab east of the Jordan. The generation that left Egypt has died in the wilderness, and their children now stand where their parents refused to go forty years earlier (Numbers 13-14). Everything depends on whether the promises made to Moses will continue under a new leader. This chapter answers that question with God's own word: the promise stands, the land is given, and the presence that went with Moses will go with Joshua. The chapter also establishes the terms of the whole book: courage, obedience to the written law, and the unity of all twelve tribes.
historical:
The date of these events depends on the date of the exodus. Those who take 1 Kings 6:1 as a straightforward count place the crossing of the Jordan around 1406 BC; many others place it in the thirteenth century BC. Either way, this is the Late Bronze Age, when Canaan was divided among small city-states under a loose Egyptian overlordship.

The territory God describes in verse 4 is vast: from the wilderness in the south to Lebanon in the north, from the Euphrates River in the east to the Great Sea (the Mediterranean) in the west, called all the land of the Hittites. The Hittites were a great empire centered in Anatolia (modern Turkey), and Hittite was also used in the region as a general name for peoples of Syria and the north. Israel never controlled all of this territory in Joshua's day. The closest it came was under David and Solomon (1 Kings 4:21, 24), and even then much of the region was held through tributary relationships rather than settlement. The eastern tribes, Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, had already received land east of the Jordan after the defeat of Sihon and Og (Numbers 32).
cultural:
The officers Joshua addresses (verse 10) were administrators, probably responsible for records and organization, who appear in Deuteronomy alongside judges and elders (Deuteronomy 16:18). Their job here is practical: telling families to prepare provisions for the crossing. Manna was still falling (it stops only in Joshua 5:12), but people would need food for travel and a campaign.

The Book of the Law in verse 8 is the written instruction of Moses, which Deuteronomy 31:9 and 31:24-26 say Moses wrote down and entrusted to the priests. Deuteronomy 17:18-20 had required any future king to keep a copy and read it all his life. Joshua is treated much as that ideal ruler: his success depends not on military skill but on faithful attention to God's word. Meditation in Israel was not silent emptying of the mind but murmuring the text aloud, repeating and pondering it, often from memory. The pledge of the eastern tribes echoes the form of loyalty oaths sworn to rulers in the ancient world, including the death penalty for rebellion (verse 18).
literary: The chapter is built of four speeches. The LORD speaks to Joshua (verses 1-9), Joshua speaks to the officers (verses 10-11), Joshua speaks to the eastern tribes (verses 12-15), and those tribes answer Joshua (verses 16-18). The command to be strong and courageous is the refrain that binds them: God says it three times (verses 6, 7, 9), and the people say it a fourth time as their last words (verse 18). The divine speech moves from promise (the land is given, God will be with you) to condition (obey the law, turn neither right nor left) and back to promise (the LORD is with you wherever you go). The name of Moses appears again and again, a sign that the book sees Joshua as continuing Moses' work, not replacing it.

outline.t: The LORD's promise: the land and his presence
Be strong and courageous; keep the Book of the Law
Joshua orders the people to prepare
The eastern tribes reminded of their promise
The people pledge obedience to Joshua

doctrines.note: Joshua's success is tied to the written word: the Book of the Law must not depart from his mouth. God's people are shaped by Scripture read, spoken, and pondered continually, not only by leaders or experiences.
God promises to be with Joshua as he was with Moses and never to leave or forsake him. His presence, not Joshua's ability, is the ground of courage.
The land is given because God swore it to the fathers (verse 6). The book begins by rooting the conquest in God's covenant faithfulness to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

The eastern tribes, already settled, must still cross and fight for their brothers until all have rest. God's people are one body, and those who have received first are called to labor for those still waiting.

words.note: Hagah, to murmur, mutter, or meditate. The same verb describes a lion growling over its prey (Isaiah 31:4) and a dove moaning (Isaiah 38:14). Meditation on the law meant speaking it under the breath, repeating it, and dwelling on it. Psalm 1:2 uses the same word for the one who meditates on the law day and night.

Sakal, to act wisely, prudently, or with success. Verses 7 and 8 promise that obedience leads to this kind of prospering. The word includes insight and skill, not just outcome, which keeps the promise from being a simple formula for material gain.

Chazaq, to be strong, paired with amats, to be courageous or firm. This pair forms the refrain of the chapter, as it did in Deuteronomy 31. The strength is steadiness in obedience as much as bravery in battle, and verse 7 connects it directly to careful keeping of the law.

Natan, to give. The land is repeatedly described as something God is giving (verses 2, 3, 6, 11, 13, 15). Israel will fight, but the land is a gift, not an achievement, and that framing governs the whole book.

christ: Joshua's name in Hebrew, Yehoshua, means the LORD saves. Its Greek form is Iesous, the same name given to Jesus. The New Testament does not treat Joshua as a coded picture of Christ, but it does draw an explicit comparison. Hebrews 4:8 says that if Joshua had given Israel final rest, God would not have spoken of another day, and it goes on to say that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God. The rest Joshua began to give (1:13-15) was real, but partial. The promise of God's presence in verse 5, “I will never leave you nor forsake you,” is quoted in Hebrews 13:5 and applied to every believer. Jesus himself, facing temptation in the wilderness, answered from the Book of the Law, from Deuteronomy, showing the kind of life with Scripture in the mouth that Joshua 1:8 describes.
questions: God commands Joshua three times to be strong and courageous. What situation in your life calls for courage that rests on God's presence rather than your own strength?
Joshua's success is tied to meditating on God's word day and night. What would it look like for Scripture to be that close to your daily life?
The eastern tribes had to fight for their brothers before enjoying their own rest. Where might God be calling you to labor for others before settling into your own comfort?
